sections.text: Phoenician and Punic settlements and exchange networks are important to southern Iberian history, but commercial influence is not blanket sovereignty. Inland relationships connect the valley with Oretanian and other regional communities. The great Barcid conquests begin later, and Roman provincial government is more distant still. Neither should be treated as the already settled political framework of the opening.

sections.title: An established southern society
sections.text: The starting faction preserves a recognizable southern river-region identity without reviving a legendary kingdom as a documented 278 state. The political future remains open among local communities and external powers. The legacy of Tartessos supplies historical depth, while the specific relationships of the opening require their own evidence rather than inherited assumptions.

bastetani.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
bastetani.text: The Bastetanian world centres on southeastern Iberian communities whose archaeology includes fortified settlements, elite burials and striking sculpture. Basti, near modern Baza, is an important regional association. By 278 BCE these communities inherit a substantial fourth-century past, while their precise common political organization is less certain than the richness of the material evidence they have left.
bastetani.homeland: Southeastern Iberian interior, including the Basti–Baza setting
bastetani.politicalForm: Regional communities with fortified centres and local elites

sections.title: The fourth-century regional background
sections.text: Settlements and cemeteries demonstrate an established Iberian society before the campaign date. The Dama de Baza belongs to the fourth century BCE and preserves evidence of elite funerary representation. Such objects reveal social distinction and ritual without identifying one dynasty ruling the entire region. A woman's prominent burial should not be reduced to a decorative artifact or converted into an undocumented national queen.

sections.title: Fortified centres and inland routes
sections.text: Basti and other regional centres stand within a southeastern landscape connected to coastal and interior routes. Fortified settlements, agricultural districts and burial grounds form different parts of that social world. The territory described by later authors is not necessarily one fixed 278 state. Neighbouring southern and eastern Iberian communities retain their own local traditions and political interests.

sections.title: Elite households and community organization
sections.text: Rich funerary contexts indicate differentiated social roles and the ability of leading groups to mobilize resources. Greek objects in graves show selective adoption and exchange, not Greek political control. The exact relation between local centres remains uncertain, and no complete spring office list survives. Local elites and settlement communities provide a defensible internal framework without a fabricated royal genealogy.

sections.title: Southern and Mediterranean connections
sections.text: Contacts with other Iberian centres and with Greek and Punic exchange link the region to a wider world. Those contacts can shape display and production while leaving local identities intact. The Barcid territorial expansion and foundation of later Punic strategic centres lie after the opening. The presence of imported goods is therefore not a reason to begin with direct Carthaginian government over the whole interior.

sections.title: A local world with a deep past
sections.text: The faction begins as a credible southeastern community grouping with substantial archaeological history. Its cultural setting remains distinct from a generic Celtiberian label. Later conquest and Roman urban development are not starting institutions, while the exact degree of political unity among the local centres remains open to qualification.

contestani.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
contestani.text: Contestanian-associated communities occupy part of eastern and southeastern Iberia, where fortified settlements and Mediterranean contacts shaped local development. The name comes from later geographical classifications, while archaeology supplies a much richer story of particular centres and their changing fortunes. In 278 BCE the relevant landscape is one of indigenous political communities, not a fully formed Carthaginian or Roman provincial administration.
contestani.homeland: Eastern and southeastern Iberian districts associated with Contestania
contestani.politicalForm: Several Iberian settlement communities and local centres

sections.title: Earlier centres and changing settlement
sections.text: The eastern Iberian archaeological record includes substantial fourth-century settlements, craft production and social differentiation. La Bastida de les Alcusses illustrates how an important centre could flourish and then be abandoned before the opening. Its remains must not be treated as an active 278 capital simply because they are well preserved. Regional history involves change among settlements, not an unbroken list of permanent city-states.

sections.title: The eastern Iberian setting
sections.text: Coastal access and routes toward inland valleys link local communities with wider exchange. Settlement hierarchies differ across the region. The later geographical label Contestania is useful for broad association but does not settle the boundaries or dependency of every place in the third century. Indigenous cities and countryside must remain distinguishable from nearby foreign commercial connections.

sections.title: Internal conditions at the opening
sections.text: Fortification, elite residences and production contexts indicate organized communities with differences in power and status. A regional label does not by itself establish one central king or an identical government in every settlement. The most substantial internal history comes from the development and replacement of local centres. Exact spring leaders remain less securely known than the archaeological evidence for community life.

sections.title: Mediterranean exchange and regional neighbours
sections.text: Greek and Punic contacts can affect imported goods and local practices without establishing sovereignty. Neighbouring Iberian communities provide other important relationships. Hamilcar's later conquest programme should not be projected into 278, and an entire coastal region cannot be made Carthaginian merely because Punic traders operate there. Local authority remains a meaningful part of the opening world.

sections.title: An indigenous eastern starting position
sections.text: The faction represents a plausible regional association rather than a claim that all later Contestanian places form one documented state at this date. Its background is rooted in local settlement history and connections. Later colonial foundations, conquests and administrative boundaries remain later developments rather than inherited starting possessions.

edetani.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
edetani.text: The Edetanian setting belongs to eastern Iberia, where settlements such as Edeta connect urban centres with agricultural hinterlands and smaller dependent sites. Archaeology gives this region a detailed social landscape before Roman conquest. The early third-century picture should not be replaced by the biography of later named war leaders or by the territorial arrangements of Roman imperial Valencia.
edetani.homeland: The eastern Iberian districts associated with Edeta and its wider setting
edetani.politicalForm: Iberian settlement centres with local political hierarchies

sections.title: The formation of a regional centre
sections.text: Edeta's development forms part of the wider rise of Iberian settlement centres during the first millennium BCE. Excavated material reveals connections among civic life, local production and social display. The name Edetani becomes clearer through later literary geography, but the region's communities have an earlier history of their own. They should not begin as an unnamed population belonging automatically to a future conqueror.

sections.title: A centre and its surrounding communities
sections.text: The relation between a prominent settlement and smaller surrounding sites is important to understanding eastern Iberian power. Agricultural districts and routes toward the coast support more than the central settlement alone. An urban centre's influence is not necessarily uniform at every distance, and the surviving hierarchy may change between periods. A later regional boundary is therefore not a precise third-century land register.

sections.title: Local elites and political authority
sections.text: Decorated objects, houses and settlement organization reveal a differentiated society. Elite influence can be substantial without proving the exact title or genealogy of its leaders in 278. Edeco and other names familiar from later military history belong to their own chronology. The opening can acknowledge organized local power without borrowing those later figures or assuming every community is governed identically.

sections.title: The eastern Iberian network
sections.text: Neighbouring Iberian communities and Mediterranean exchange place the region within several overlapping networks. Imported pottery or artistic styles do not by themselves mark a foreign state boundary. Carthaginian territorial expansion later in the third century changes the balance, but that programme has not begun at this opening. Roman presence in the peninsula is likewise not yet the provincial order of later centuries.

sections.title: Before the Punic-war political map
sections.text: The faction's starting identity rests on the indigenous Edetanian setting rather than on later alliances with Mediterranean armies. Exact inter-settlement dependencies and borders remain open to refinement. The historical background gives the region its own origins and social structure while leaving subsequent diplomatic and military choices to the unfolding campaign.

ilergetes.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
ilergetes.text: The Ilergetan setting lies in northeastern Iberia around the Segre and neighbouring river districts. It connects interior routes with the wider Ebro world. The faction's familiar historical identity becomes especially visible during later conflicts involving Carthage and Rome, but in 278 BCE its local communities belong to an earlier political landscape with their own settlement development and regional interests.
ilergetes.homeland: The Segre and neighbouring northeastern Iberian interior
ilergetes.politicalForm: Iberian regional communities and significant settlement centres

sections.title: Local development before the war narratives
sections.text: Archaeological collections document Iron Age communities in the region before the named leaders of the Punic-war period enter the literary record. The rise and organization of local centres must be understood on their own chronology. Later accounts give the Ilergetes a stronger narrative presence, but do not mean their earlier history consisted only of preparations for those external wars.

sections.title: Rivers and the northeastern interior
sections.text: The Segre and connected routes link local agricultural districts with the Ebro basin and surrounding uplands. Ilerda becomes an important historical place association, while Roman municipal development belongs later. Connections toward other Iberian communities do not remove local distinctions. The region's position allows contact between inland and coastal networks without proving that a coastal Greek city controls it.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: The evidence supports communities capable of settlement organization, production and regional interaction. It does not supply a complete spring governing roster. Indibilis and Mandonius belong to later events and should not be installed as starting leaders. The degree of coordination among centres may be approximated for the faction without claiming that later descriptions establish every earlier constitutional detail.

sections.title: The Ebro-connected political world
sections.text: Neighbouring interior and northeastern Iberian groups provide the most immediate external relationships. Greek coastal exchange and wider Mediterranean contacts add other connections, but are not automatic ownership. The struggle between Rome and Carthage that later makes the region strategically prominent has not yet arrived. Its communities therefore begin with local room for action rather than a compulsory role as auxiliaries in that later conflict.

sections.title: A northeastern interior faction
sections.text: The opening preserves the Ilergetan regional association while separating its earlier setting from the better documented late-third-century narrative. Local identity and political allocation remain distinct from imported material culture. Later campaigns, named leaders and changes of allegiance are not starting facts merely because they are the best known episodes of the region's history.

indigetes.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
indigetes.text: The Indigete setting in northeastern Iberia is unusually well illuminated by archaeology at Ullastret. This is not simply a vague tribal background behind Greek coastal settlements: substantial fortified centres, agricultural organization and elite activity give the local society its own political depth. Around 278 BCE it stands beside Greek communities such as Emporion without being identical to them.
indigetes.homeland: The northeastern Iberian coastal hinterland around Ullastret and the Empordà setting
indigetes.politicalForm: Iberian communities with major centres and developing regional hierarchies

sections.title: The growth of Ullastret
sections.text: Settlement at Ullastret developed from the sixth century BCE and expanded into one of the peninsula's major pre-Roman centres. The nearby complex includes more than a single hilltop site, with associated settlement at Illa d'en Reixac. Ancient authors later connect the region with the Indigetes. Archaeology gives that broad association a substantive local history without resolving every question of ethnic naming.

sections.title: An Iberian hinterland beside Greek ports
sections.text: Fortified centres, agricultural land and routes toward the coast link the inland communities with Emporion and other maritime contacts. Greek imports reveal exchange and influence, but not the disappearance of Iberian identity. Nor should the enclosing indigenous regional envelope establish that Greek Emporion or Rhode is politically governed in the same way as Ullastret.

sections.title: Settlement hierarchy and elite power
sections.text: Archaeological research identifies changes in settlement hierarchy and concentration of power during the centuries before the opening. Fortifications, enlarged urban areas and differentiated residences provide more evidence than a generic tribal label conveys. Interpretation of the precise state form remains a scholarly question. An exact spring royal roster is not preserved, but the society is clearly more organized than an undifferentiated collection of isolated farmsteads.

sections.title: Exchange without automatic dependence
sections.text: Greek coastal connections are central to the regional story, alongside relationships with other Iberian communities. Trade may strengthen local elites as well as foreign merchants. Rome and Carthage later transform the northeastern balance, but their subsequent conflict should not be projected into 278. The opening leaves Greek civic communities recognizable while preserving the substantial indigenous political landscape around them.

sections.title: A substantial local society
sections.text: The faction begins with a credible northeastern homeland and a developed archaeological past. The degree of regional centralization is qualified rather than ignored. Ullastret's later abandonment and Roman-period reorganization are not predetermined current events, and colonial connections alone do not dictate ownership of its neighbouring Greek settlements.

arverni.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
arverni.text: The Arvernian faction belongs to the uplands and basins of central Gaul, especially the Auvergne setting. Its later prominence should not obscure the earlier regional communities represented in 278 BCE. The power of second-century kings and the career of Vercingetorix lie in the future; the opening instead concerns the development of local authority, regional resources and connections across a changing Iron Age world.
arverni.homeland: The Auvergne and central Gallic uplands
arverni.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities; the exact early political centre is uncertain

sections.title: The region before its famous rulers
sections.text: Arvernian power becomes especially visible in later accounts of central Gaul. Archaeology supplies a much longer history of occupation and changing centres. Corent, Gondole and Gergovie are important to that research, but their mature later political roles cannot all be assigned to 278. A regional identity is not a guarantee of an unchanged capital or dynasty over several centuries.

sections.title: Uplands, basins and movement
sections.text: The central landscape combines defensible heights, agricultural basins and routes toward surrounding river systems. Communities depend on more than military strongholds: production, farming and gatherings connect their local worlds. The wealth later associated with Arvernian elites has regional foundations, but its documented later scale should not become a precise opening treasury or an already established empire over all Gaul.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: The evidence supports local authority and social differentiation more securely than an exact spring royal succession. Later banqueting, coinage and public institutions belong to dated phases of development. Leading households and community coordination are plausible, but familiar second-century kings cannot be installed early. The central question is the growth of regional power, not the operation of a fully recovered contemporary constitution.

sections.title: Connections across central Gaul
sections.text: Relationships extend toward neighbouring communities and routes leading to Mediterranean exchange. Later rivalry with the Aedui is historically important, but should not be turned into an eternal opening war. Rome is still occupied with an Italian conflict and has not established its later Gallic province. Shared Celtic cultural practices likewise do not place all neighbouring populations under one Arvernian command.

sections.title: A central Gallic beginning
sections.text: Spring 278 represents an earlier stage of the region's history than the oppida and leaders best known from the last century of Gallic independence. Its inhabitants have substantial local traditions and room for political development. Later supremacy, conquest and resistance remain possible historical comparisons rather than accomplishments already possessed at the start.

aedui.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
aedui.text: The Aeduan setting lies in central-eastern Gaul, connected with routes through the Saône world. It later becomes one of the most prominent political communities in Caesar's narrative. The opening is considerably earlier: its local societies and regional connections matter, while the large town of Bibracte, familiar magistracies and Roman friendship require their own chronology rather than automatic transfer into 278 BCE.
aedui.homeland: Central-eastern Gaul and the Saône-connected interior
aedui.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities before the fully documented later Aeduan state

sections.title: Before Bibracte's urban age
sections.text: The landscape has an Iron Age history predating the later Aeduan capital. Bibracte's major town belongs to the second and first centuries BCE, making it a particularly clear chronological warning. Earlier communities should not be presented as inhabiting its mature streets and workshops in 278. The development of regional identity and the rise of a famous urban centre are connected but separate processes.

sections.title: An inland crossroads
sections.text: Routes associated with the Saône and neighbouring interior districts connect the region with wider Gallic and Mediterranean movement. Agricultural settlements, local production and circulation of goods provide a stronger early foundation than a picture based entirely on Caesar's cities. The importance of those routes can be recognized without assuming that every later toll, market or political dependency already operates at the opening.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: The later Aeduan political system is unusually visible through outside accounts, including elite competition and civic offices. Those details cannot supply a complete earlier government. Local leading groups and shared interests are plausible, but the precise institutional form of 278 is incompletely known. Changes in settlement scale and elite expression are part of the history, rather than evidence that society remained politically unchanged.

sections.title: Neighbours before Roman provincial power
sections.text: The Arvernian, Sequanian and other regional worlds provide different routes for cooperation and rivalry. Later Roman descriptions of Aeduan friendship and political precedence belong to a changed international setting. They do not establish a Roman protectorate in 278. Nor does a shared Gallic identity imply a common foreign policy binding every community in central-eastern Gaul.

sections.title: An earlier Aeduan setting
sections.text: The faction begins with a credible regional association and an inhabited countryside, rather than the entire late-Republican political order. Bibracte's later fame remains part of the historical perspective, not a starting urban achievement. Its future institutions and alliances are developments to distinguish from the communities present in the early third century.

bituriges.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
bituriges.text: The Biturigan name is associated with central Gaul and, in later geography, with a separate Vivisci community around Burdigala. Those associations should not be mistaken for proof of one kingdom joining Berry to the Atlantic in 278 BCE. The faction's regional reconstruction sits within a much older history of settlements, exchange and changing centres of power.
bituriges.homeland: Central Gaul; the separate later Vivisci association around Burdigala is qualified
bituriges.politicalForm: Regional communities; Cubi and Vivisci are not assumed to form one documented state

sections.title: A name with more than one regional setting
sections.text: The later Bituriges Cubi are strongly connected with the central Gallic setting around Avaricum, while the Vivisci appear around Burdigala. Ancient accounts do not justify treating every shared ethnonym as a single sovereign system. The relationship and chronology of the two associations must remain distinct. Legends of very early Biturigan predominance likewise require a different evidential status from archaeological settlement history.

sections.title: Bourges and the central landscape
sections.text: Archaeology around Bourges records significant early Iron Age activity and contacts before the later fortified town of Caesar's period. That longer sequence gives the region depth without making every urban phase contemporary. River routes and surrounding agricultural districts connect local communities with wider central Gaul. Burdigala's Atlantic setting presents a different local history and cannot simply be treated as another district of the same early capital.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Settlement and elite evidence show that local societies can be organized and differentiated even where a precise royal chronology is absent. The available record does not establish a complete spring constitution linking all Biturigan associations. Local leadership and regional centres are the more secure foundations. The mature political and military organization visible during Rome's conquest belongs to a later stage.

sections.title: Central and Atlantic relationships
sections.text: Central communities connect with neighbouring Gallic regions, while the Burdigala setting faces the Garonne and Aquitanian world. Those relationships are not identical. Strabo explicitly distinguishes the Vivisci's cultural association from surrounding Aquitanian peoples. Neither geographic proximity nor the sharing of a name establishes permanent alliance, tribute or ownership at the campaign opening.

sections.title: A qualified regional representation
sections.text: The opening retains a recognizable Biturigan identity while documenting the distinction between later branches. Burdigala's allocation is a broad regional approximation rather than proof of a united trans-Gallic monarchy. The historical account preserves the difference between a name, a cultural association and a specific political relationship in spring 278.

carnutes.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
carnutes.text: The Carnutian setting is associated with the middle Loire and neighbouring interior routes of Gaul. Later accounts make the Carnutes prominent in political and religious history, especially around Cenabum and gatherings attributed to druids. In 278 BCE those later descriptions cannot simply be treated as a complete account of an already mature state, but the earlier river-region communities have a substantial history of their own.
carnutes.homeland: The middle Loire and adjoining interior Gallic districts
carnutes.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities; exact early common institutions are unknown

sections.title: The region before Caesar's narrative
sections.text: The later ethnonym identifies a recognizable central Gallic population, but literary detail becomes much fuller in the first century BCE. Local Iron Age development precedes that visibility. The stories of religious gatherings are important evidence for the period described, not proof that the same centralized arrangement operated unchanged two centuries earlier. The distinction allows an earlier community history without inventing an undocumented foundation.

sections.title: The Loire as a connecting route
sections.text: River movement, crossings and adjoining agricultural districts give the region strategic value beyond one town. Cenabum is an important later civic and commercial association. Its setting connects northern and central routes without making it a detached modern city-state in an otherwise empty countryside. The larger political importance of such places may change as settlement and exchange networks develop.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Local leading groups and religious activity can help connect communities, but the sources do not supply a reliable spring office list. A druids' gathering described later should not become a governing cabinet ruling all central Gaul. Authority over land, gatherings and exchange may be distributed among several communities. Cultural commonality is therefore not a substitute for evidence of one sovereign hierarchy.

sections.title: A central position among neighbours
sections.text: The river-region communities connect with Aulerci, Biturigan-associated and other Gallic settings. Such neighbours need not be permanently hostile or allied. Rome's later intervention and the famous events at Cenabum belong to a different political world. Spring 278 is earlier than the provincial and campaigning arrangements that make those events possible.

sections.title: Cenabum within its regional context
sections.text: The opening associates Cenabum with the existing Carnutian grouping rather than an unrelated regional controller. That allocation remains a reconstruction of an earlier landscape, not a claim that later boundaries and institutions are certain. The faction's regional identity can remain coherent while its exact third-century degree of political unity is left unresolved.

senones-gaul.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
senones-gaul.text: This faction represents the Senonian association in Gaul, particularly the Yonne-connected interior. It must be distinguished from the Senones established in Italy and defeated by Rome before the campaign opening. Shared names and migration traditions connect parts of the historical record, but they do not establish a single state stretching across the Alps or mean that the Gallic communities disappeared with the Italian defeat.
senones-gaul.homeland: The Yonne-connected interior of northern Gaul
senones-gaul.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities distinct from the Italian Senones

sections.title: Names, migration and separate histories
sections.text: Later ancient accounts link Senonian names with both Gaul and the history of Gallic movements into Italy. The tradition surrounding the sack of Rome belongs to that wider narrative, but does not give a precise genealogy for every community using the name. Local societies in Gaul retain their own development and cannot be reduced to a surviving branch of one centrally directed migration.

sections.title: The Yonne and northern interior
sections.text: Routes along the Yonne connect the regional setting with the Seine basin and central Gaul. Agedincum becomes a familiar later place association, while its Roman urban identity belongs to another period. Farming communities and local connections provide the earlier foundation. The boundaries of a later civic territory are not a complete map of authority in 278.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: The surviving evidence does not identify one certain starting ruler or an unchanging institution inherited from the migration stories. Local leadership and coordination among communities are more defensible. Later political figures in Caesar's account belong to their own generation. The region's society may be organized and stratified without the details of its spring decision-making being recoverable.

sections.title: Neighbours and the distant Italian wars
sections.text: Northern and central Gallic routes connect the faction's setting with other regional communities. Rome's destruction of Italian Senonian power is relevant background, but not evidence that the Gallic Senones are already a Roman dependency or currently fighting the same war. Cultural and kinship traditions can cross distances without creating one chain of political command.

sections.title: A Gallic rather than Italian controller
sections.text: The opening preserves the stable Gallic Senonian identity and its homeland. It does not revive a conquered Italian territory or treat a shared name as an automatic overseas claim. Later Roman conquest of Gaul remains outside the starting situation, while the precise early institutions and frontiers remain qualified.

parisii.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
parisii.text: The Parisian faction belongs to the Seine-region communities later known as the Parisii. It is not the government of a modern capital projected into antiquity. The opening concerns a river landscape and its local societies well before the documented world of Caesar, the development of Roman Lutetia or the political importance of medieval and modern Paris.
parisii.homeland: The Seine setting associated with the later Parisii and Lutetia
parisii.politicalForm: Regional communities; the early urban and political centre is uncertain

sections.title: An earlier Seine landscape
sections.text: Settlement and movement along the Seine have a history much older than Roman written descriptions of the Parisii. The ethnonym identifies a later regional community, but does not provide a foundation date for a 278 state. Archaeological interpretations of pre-Roman centres also differ from the simple assumption that every phase was centred on the later city's most familiar island.

sections.title: River connections and local territory
sections.text: The Seine links inland districts with routes toward the Channel. Crossings and meeting places can be important without already supporting a mature Roman-style city. Local agricultural communities form part of the setting rather than an empty hinterland. The scale, location and political role of later settlements must be distinguished from what can safely be reconstructed for the early third century.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: No secure spring roster of magistrates or kings survives. Regional leading groups and cooperation around local resources are plausible, but an urban constitution cannot simply be copied from a later period. Differences in wealth and status are consistent with the wider Iron Age evidence. That does not identify a specific factional struggle or make every community subordinate to one documented capital.

sections.title: The Seine and its neighbours
sections.text: Connections reach toward other northern Gallic communities and the wider river network. The similarly named Parisii of Britain do not establish a shared trans-Channel sovereign state. Rome's military involvement in this region belongs much later. The opening's external world is therefore one of indigenous communities and routes, not a Roman provincial frontier surrounding an early Paris.

sections.title: Before Roman Lutetia
sections.text: Spring 278 uses a plausible Seine-region association while leaving precise early political boundaries open. The name helps recognition without claiming that later civic territory already exists unchanged. The community's future significance is historical perspective, not a guarantee of political leadership over northern Gaul.

remi.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
remi.text: The Remian setting lies in northeastern Gaul, connected with the Champagne region and routes between several northern communities. The Remi are especially visible in Caesar's later account as a community making its own choices amid a Belgic coalition. That evidence is valuable precisely because it shows regional diversity, but its alliances and named leaders do not describe the opening of 278 BCE.
remi.homeland: Northeastern Gaul and the later Remian–Champagne setting
remi.politicalForm: Regional communities before the fully documented late Gallic civic order

sections.title: The regional past before Roman accounts
sections.text: The northeastern Iron Age landscape contains communities whose histories precede their clear appearance in Roman narratives. Later Remian identity provides a recognizable regional association rather than an exact political foundation date. The development of settlement centres, elite relationships and collective names need not happen simultaneously. A mature first-century civic order should not be assumed to have existed unchanged for two centuries.

sections.title: The northeastern crossroads
sections.text: The region connects routes through northern and central-eastern Gaul. Agricultural districts and river-related movement matter alongside the later importance of Durocortorum. The city's familiar late Gallic and Roman phases should not define the appearance or government of the landscape in 278. Earlier local communities remain the basis of the starting population.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Caesar's named representatives reveal how a later community could negotiate collectively, but do not supply spring 278 office-holders. Local elites and broader community interests may cooperate or diverge. The exact early political structure remains incompletely known. This is a reason to distinguish stages of development, rather than to replace the inhabitants with a fictional dynasty or an unchanging tribal constitution.

sections.title: Not one permanent Belgic policy
sections.text: Later cooperation with Rome demonstrates that peoples called Belgae did not always act as one political unit. That relationship is not a starting alliance in this much earlier year. Nearby communities and long-distance contacts form the relevant regional environment. Shared classification does not eliminate diplomacy, rivalry or independent decision-making among the groups represented on the map.

sections.title: An earlier northeastern community
sections.text: The opening retains a Remian regional identity without assigning its later Roman friendship or civic privileges in advance. The people and landscape have a history of their own before the conquest narrative. Exact early borders and governing institutions remain qualified, while the faction's external choices are left open.

nervii.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
nervii.text: The Nervian setting belongs to the northern Gallic interior, associated with the Sambre–Scheldt world in later historical geography. Caesar's dramatic account of warfare gives the Nervii a strong later reputation, but its military and moral portrait is an outsider's construction. The 278 BCE opening instead requires an earlier regional society whose local settlements and relationships are only partly illuminated by that later narrative.
nervii.homeland: The northern Gallic interior around the later Sambre–Scheldt association
nervii.politicalForm: Regional northern communities; precise early collective government is uncertain

sections.title: Before the famous battle narrative
sections.text: The name becomes clear in accounts of the first-century Roman invasion of northern Gaul. Those accounts do not establish a continuous, fully formed Nervian state beginning in the third century. Archaeology places the population within longer regional developments. Descriptions of exceptional austerity or martial character must be assessed as literary claims, not adopted as timeless ethnic attributes.

sections.title: An interior northern landscape
sections.text: River routes, farming districts and connections between neighbouring communities form the regional setting. A modern national boundary cannot define an ancient tribal frontier. The later Roman civic centre and administrative district belong to subsequent developments. Neither wooded terrain in a campaign account nor its tactical use should become a complete description of how the whole population lived in 278.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: A capacity for coordinated action is plausible, but the evidence does not supply exact spring leaders or a permanent royal hierarchy. Local differentiation and regional alliances can develop over time. The later narrative concentrates on warriors and decisions during a crisis, leaving much everyday organization unrecorded. Agricultural and household communities remain part of society even where the literary sources foreground military resistance.

sections.title: The northern Gallic network
sections.text: Other Belgic-associated communities and routes toward the Rhine and central Gaul create several possible connections. Later claims of ancestry do not prove one uniform culture or a permanent interstate alliance in 278. Rome's war against the Nervii lies far in the future. The opening should therefore not begin with the specific coalition, battle or diplomatic position described for Caesar's time.

sections.title: A northern identity without a borrowed war
sections.text: The faction preserves a recognizable regional association while separating its earlier communities from the better documented conquest period. Its reputation supplies historical interest, not a fixed combat bonus or inevitable enemy. The extent of political unity in the opening year remains less secure than the existence of the region's inhabited Iron Age landscape.

belgae.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
belgae.text: Belgae is a broad regional label for several northern Gallic populations, not the name of a single enduring national government. The campaign's coastal grouping gives those communities a coherent presence without pretending that all later Belgic peoples obeyed one ruler in 278 BCE. Its setting includes local societies and routes whose histories are older than the Roman accounts that define the collective name most clearly.
belgae.homeland: Northern Gaul, with a broad coastal and northeastern regional association
belgae.politicalForm: Regional grouping of several communities; no assumed unified Belgic state

sections.title: A collective name in later geography
sections.text: Caesar distinguishes the Belgae from other broad divisions of Gaul, but also names communities with separate policies and leadership. His classification reflects the first-century world he encountered and described. Statements about ancestry cannot be converted into a precise mass-migration date for every group. The third-century setting must therefore allow indigenous continuity and political change within the broad northern association.

sections.title: Coastal and inland connections
sections.text: The northern landscape includes coastward routes, river valleys and agricultural interiors. These environments do not support one simple model of settlement or identity. Samarobriva's later Ambian association belongs within this wider regional world. Using a broad northern grouping for that place does not establish that the Ambiani were subjects of a documented national Belgic monarchy in spring 278.

sections.title: Several centres of political action
sections.text: The existence of later coalitions shows potential for coordination, but also highlights the separate communities from which they were assembled. A single permanent command should not be assumed from an occasional common war. The opening does not have a recoverable collective royal roster. Local leading groups, settlement communities and negotiated cooperation provide the more plausible internal framework.

sections.title: Across northern Gaul and the Channel
sections.text: Other Gallic regions, the Rhine-facing world and cross-Channel contacts all matter to the wider setting. Shared names or cultural forms do not establish fixed borders or overseas sovereignty. The different choices made by later Remi and Nervii demonstrate the danger of assigning one permanent foreign policy to the whole category. Rome's later conquest should not define a standing war in 278.

sections.title: A broad reconstruction with local identities
sections.text: The starting grouping keeps northern communities geographically plausible while leaving their precise third-century political relationships open. It is not modern Belgium in ancient costume. Later tribal names help recognition, but the regional faction remains a practical representation rather than a claim that every included community formed one documented sovereign state.

armorican-veneti.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
armorican-veneti.text: The Armorican Veneti are associated with the Atlantic coast of western Gaul, especially the Morbihan setting. They are distinct from the Adriatic Veneti of Italy. Their later maritime reputation is important historical context, but the opening is more than two centuries before Caesar's naval campaign: local coastal and inland communities, rather than that later war fleet, form the starting historical society.
armorican-veneti.homeland: The Atlantic Armorican coast and neighbouring inland districts
armorican-veneti.politicalForm: Regional Armorican communities; exact early common institutions are uncertain

sections.title: Armorica before the conquest narrative
sections.text: Western Gaul has a long history of settlement and Atlantic contact. The Venetic ethnonym becomes most visible through later accounts of Roman conquest. Archaeological cultural patterns should not be treated as proof that every community using similar objects already belonged to one state in 278. Equally, the absence of a detailed written narrative does not mean the coast lacked organized local societies.

sections.title: Coast, estuaries and the interior
sections.text: Access to sheltered waters and routes along the Atlantic is important, but the population should not be reduced to sailors alone. Farming and inland settlements form part of the same regional setting. Later Roman Darioritum does not provide a completed opening capital. Maritime connections can extend farther than political authority, so a trading relationship with Britain is not evidence of Venetic sovereignty there.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Control of local resources, cooperation among communities and regional leading groups offer a grounded picture. The precise institutional arrangements of the spring are not preserved. The command structure and ship descriptions from the war of 56 BCE belong to a later crisis. They cannot be transferred wholesale into the opening as a standing navy or an unchanged national constitution.

sections.title: The Atlantic network
sections.text: Britain and neighbouring Armorican communities provide potential channels for contact, while interior routes connect with the rest of Gaul. Those connections need not create a unified Atlantic confederation. Later cooperation by Pictones and Santones with Rome illustrates that coastal peoples did not all follow one policy. It does not assign those later alignments to spring 278.

sections.title: Before the Venetic war with Rome
sections.text: The opening gives the region its own indigenous coastal identity without importing Caesar's campaign as current history. The Italian and Armorican peoples remain separate despite the similar name. Their later maritime prominence supplies perspective, while the exact early borders and degree of political centralization remain qualified.

aulerci.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
aulerci.text: Aulerci is itself a broad name associated with more than one community in western and northwestern Gaul. The campaign uses it as a regional identity rather than proof of a single centrally governed kingdom in 278 BCE. The local history belongs to inland routes, farming societies and changing elite networks, with later named divisions providing a guide to geography rather than a complete early political map.
aulerci.homeland: Western and northwestern Gallic interior districts
aulerci.politicalForm: Several related regional communities grouped for the opening

sections.title: A name covering several communities
sections.text: Later accounts distinguish different Aulercan groups rather than describing one unquestioned state. The regional name therefore requires interpretation even for periods with better written evidence. The third-century population has an older local history, but the exact process by which its political identities developed is incompletely known. Shared naming should not substitute for a documented common royal genealogy.

sections.title: The western Gallic interior
sections.text: Agricultural districts and routes between river systems connect the regional communities with coastal and central Gallic worlds. They are not simply an empty buffer behind maritime Armorica. Later Roman towns and civic boundaries represent subsequent organization. Earlier settlement and social connections need to be reconstructed without assuming that those later administrative divisions already determined every local relationship.

sections.title: Local organization in 278 BCE
sections.text: The broad label allows several centres and leadership groups rather than requiring an invented national capital. Cooperation may occur through kinship, exchange, gatherings or particular military needs, but its exact form is not preserved for the opening. Material similarities and wider Celtic traditions provide context without proving one constitution. The internal society should therefore retain local variation alongside its shared regional representation.

sections.title: Between Armorica and central Gaul
sections.text: Neighbouring coastal communities and Loire-connected regions provide different directions of contact. Cultural links with groups elsewhere bearing related names do not establish common sovereignty. Roman conquest lies later, and the campaign should not begin with the specific alliances of the first-century war. Local communities retain room for their own external choices within the wider western network.

sections.title: A plural regional identity
sections.text: The Aulercan faction begins as a coherent grouping of plausible western communities, with political unity qualified rather than fabricated. The later record helps distinguish its wider setting, but does not award an exact 278 hierarchy. Its historical identity is deliberately broader than the government of one documented city.

pictones.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
pictones.text: The Pictonian setting occupies part of western Gaul, linking an Atlantic-facing region with routes into the interior. Later Roman accounts and the development of Lemonum make the name familiar, but the opening belongs to an earlier society of local communities. In 278 BCE its relationships are not already those of a Roman allied or provincial population.
pictones.homeland: Western Gaul in the later Poitou and lower-Loire-facing setting
pictones.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities with incompletely known early institutions

sections.title: The region before Roman political history
sections.text: The local Iron Age landscape developed before the Pictones acquired a fuller narrative in Roman sources. Later place and people names identify a regional association, not a single recorded foundation of a state. Changes in settlement, elite organization and exchange must be given their own chronology. The mature Roman town of Lemonum is not a complete description of the region's earlier political centre.

sections.title: The Atlantic-facing western interior
sections.text: River routes connect agricultural districts with the coast and neighbouring regions. The location gives access to several different networks rather than only one seaward direction. Communities in the interior remain important to local resources and authority. The modern name Poitou is useful orientation, but its later boundaries cannot establish the reach of a political unit in 278.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: The available evidence does not identify a secure spring royal succession or a uniform government over all associated settlements. Leading groups and community cooperation are plausible within the wider Gallic setting. Later coinage and civic status can illuminate subsequent development without being granted automatically to the opening. Political organization has a history rather than one timeless tribal form.

sections.title: Neighbours and maritime possibilities
sections.text: The Santonian, Aulercan and other western regions form part of the immediate environment. Later involvement in Rome's naval operations against the Veneti demonstrates that Atlantic-facing peoples could choose different alignments. That particular cooperation belongs to the first century BCE, not spring 278. Contact and exchange remain meaningful without requiring an already established Roman military partnership.

sections.title: An earlier western Gallic community
sections.text: The faction starts from a credible regional homeland and the local societies preceding Roman conquest. Its later civic identity and alliances are not starting privileges. The exact extent of early collective rule remains uncertain, while the region's position between coastal and interior routes gives it a clear historical character.

santones.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
santones.text: The Santonian setting lies in western Gaul around the Charente-connected world and approaches to the Garonne estuary. It stands near a major transition between Gallic and Aquitanian regional associations. By 278 BCE this is an inhabited and connected landscape, but the political and urban arrangements known from later Saintes and Roman geography must be separated from the earlier communities represented at the start.
santones.homeland: Western Gaul near the Charente and the northern side of the Garonne-estuary setting
santones.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities before the later documented civic order

sections.title: A regional identity before the Roman town
sections.text: Later geographers place the Santones beside Atlantic and estuarine routes. Their name helps identify a regional history older than Roman administration, but does not date every stage of settlement centralization. The later prominence of Mediolanum Santonum should not supply an already Romanized capital in 278. Earlier agricultural and local communities remain part of the historical foundation.

sections.title: Rivers and the estuarine neighbourhood
sections.text: Routes associated with the Charente and Garonne approaches connect maritime and inland movement. Strabo distinguishes nearby Bituriges Vivisci and Aquitanian populations, showing that proximity does not mean uniform identity. The estuary offers exchange opportunities but is not a political boundary that can be read directly from a modern map. Its communities may participate in several overlapping networks.

sections.title: Internal conditions at the opening
sections.text: The exact third-century structure of common authority is not preserved. Local leading groups and settlement communities provide a plausible basis, while later civic institutions require separate evidence. Social and cultural similarities with other Gauls do not establish one national government. The important internal context is an organized regional population whose political development should not be flattened into the later Roman administrative scheme.

sections.title: Between Atlantic and Aquitanian worlds
sections.text: Contacts reach toward the Pictones, the Garonne region and wider western routes. Later participation in Rome's war against the Veneti is not a permanent ancient alliance. Neither the Santones nor the Vivisci can be assigned sovereignty over every settlement near the estuary simply by cultural resemblance. The early external picture is one of local and regional relationships rather than a settled Roman sphere.

sections.title: A western region with distinct neighbours
sections.text: The starting community remains separate from both the Aquitanian grouping and the later Vivisci association. It does not inherit all neighbouring coastal sites merely because their exact early control is uncertain. Its historical setting is defined by local continuity and useful connections, with later alliances and urban institutions left in their proper periods.

aquitani.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
aquitani.text: The Aquitanian grouping represents indigenous communities between the Garonne and the Pyrenees, rather than one uniform Gallic kingdom. Ancient writers distinguish their speech and identity from neighbouring Gauls, while later inscriptions preserve a distinctive onomastic record. In 278 BCE the region should retain that difference without pretending that every later people-name, dialect boundary or political relationship can be mapped precisely.
aquitani.homeland: Southwestern communities between the Garonne and the Pyrenees
aquitani.politicalForm: Several regional communities rather than an assumed unified Aquitanian state

sections.title: A regional history distinct from generic Gaul
sections.text: The ancient category Aquitani is not identical to the later enlarged Roman province of Aquitania. Caesar and Strabo distinguish populations south of the Garonne from neighbouring Gallic communities. Their observations are later than 278, but warn against erasing regional differences. Connections between later Aquitanian name evidence and the history of Basque also require linguistic interpretation, not a simple claim of one ancient modern-shaped nation.

sections.title: Atlantic lowlands and Pyrenean districts
sections.text: The landscape combines coastward areas, river valleys and mountain-facing communities. Those different environments support local variation rather than a single identical way of life. Contacts toward Iberia and the Pyrenees can coexist with exchange across the Garonne. Neither a modern regional boundary nor a broad cultural classification establishes the exact jurisdiction of every local centre in 278.

sections.title: A plural political landscape
sections.text: Later accounts describe numerous communities, making a single undifferentiated monarchy especially difficult to justify. Local leaders and groups can cooperate without permanent regional centralization. The opening's precise governing relationships are not preserved. Recognizing that plurality provides more historical substance than assigning everyone the institutions of a neighbouring Gallic people or replacing the region with a foreign state.

sections.title: The Garonne as contact zone
sections.text: Gallic populations north of the river and the later Vivisci association around Burdigala illustrate a varied neighbourhood. Strabo's account explicitly prevents a simple equation of location with culture or tribute. Pyrenean connections add another direction of contact. Rome's later administrative expansion of Aquitania should not be mistaken for indigenous political unity in the early third century BCE.

sections.title: Indigenous communities at the start
sections.text: The regional faction preserves a southwestern identity distinct from generic Gallic classification. It does not claim that all included communities formed one documented sovereign state or spoke one precisely reconstructed dialect. The opening's broad association remains usable while local cultural and political distinctions stay available for later refinement.

volcae.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
volcae.text: The Volcaean setting belongs to southern Gaul, including regional associations around Tolosa and the wider Mediterranean-facing interior. Later sources distinguish several Volcaean groups, while similarly named Tectosages also appear in Galatian migration history. These connections should not become a single state stretching from Gaul to Anatolia. The early third-century setting is one of regional development and movement rather than fixed later frontiers.
volcae.homeland: Southern Gallic districts, including the later Tolosa-associated setting
volcae.politicalForm: Related southern Gallic communities; exact early organization and settlement chronology are qualified

sections.title: Southern settlement and changing identities
sections.text: The Volcaean names belong to the complex history of Celtic movement and local development in southern Gaul. Later divisions such as Tectosages and Arecomici help identify different associations, but their full later political geography should not be assumed at the start. Similar names appearing far apart may preserve historical connections without demonstrating continuing shared government.

sections.title: Tolosa and the southern routes
sections.text: The Tolosa setting connects interior movement with routes toward the Mediterranean and western river systems. It is not a detached Anatolian possession. Southern Gaul also contains Greek coastal communities and indigenous populations with their own histories. Shared exchange networks do not establish that the Volcae control every port or neighbouring settlement, and later Roman provincial boundaries are a separate development.

sections.title: Internal position in 278 BCE
sections.text: Local communities and changing regional leadership are more defensible than one perfectly known confederal constitution. Migration narratives alone cannot tell how every settlement was governed. The precise stage of southern Volcaean settlement and organization around 278 remains qualified. That uncertainty should coexist with the reality of established local populations rather than being filled with a fictional dynasty or a foreign controller.

sections.title: Gaul and the Galatian connection
sections.text: Movements toward the Balkans and Anatolia form part of the wider Celtic history of the period. The groups retained as pending Galatian arrivals are not automatically rulers of Tolosa, nor do they own settled Anatolian territories in this spring convention. Local southern relationships with Greek and indigenous neighbours remain distinct from the diplomacy of migrant military groups far to the east.

sections.title: A southern Gallic association
sections.text: The opening associates Tolosa with an existing southern regional faction instead of using a distant migration identity as its controller. This is a plausible reconstruction rather than proof of exact third-century borders. Later Roman conquest and the fully developed political arrangements of the Tectosages or Arecomici are not assumed to be completed starting facts.

allobroges.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
allobroges.text: The Allobrogian setting connects the upper Rhone, Alpine approaches and the country associated with the Isère. It is a strategically important region whose later political history is better documented than its organization in 278 BCE. The faction represents earlier local communities within that landscape, rather than importing the alliances, urban centres and provincial relationships of a later century unchanged.
allobroges.homeland: Upper-Rhone and Isère-associated districts near the western Alpine approaches
allobroges.politicalForm: Regional Gallic communities with uncertain early collective institutions

sections.title: An Alpine-facing regional identity
sections.text: Later authors identify the Allobroges in the southeastern Gallic world. Their accounts give useful geography but do not provide a complete earlier political genealogy. Archaeological development in the region extends beyond the events recorded by Mediterranean historians. The emergence of collective names, central places and broader leadership should therefore be understood as historical processes, not one timeless tribal arrangement.

sections.title: Rivers and approaches to the Alps
sections.text: The Rhone and connected valleys provide routes between Alpine, interior and Mediterranean-facing worlds. Agricultural communities and exchange matter alongside the military usefulness of crossings. Vienne's better documented later importance cannot define every aspect of settlement in 278. The landscape has several possible centres of local authority rather than one automatically recoverable capital.

sections.title: Internal position at the opening
sections.text: The early regional society can be described through local communities and influential groups, but the exact structure of shared leadership remains uncertain. Later named kings and magistrates belong to their own periods. Cultural connections with other Gallic peoples do not eliminate local variation. A coherent regional faction need not imply that a complete central government is documented for this particular spring.

sections.title: A meeting place of routes
sections.text: Contacts extend toward Alpine communities, the interior of Gaul and the southern coast. Hannibal's later passage and Roman campaigns make the region prominent in subsequent history, but do not establish a current Carthaginian alliance or Roman dependency in 278. Geography creates opportunities and pressures without fixing one foreign policy across every generation.

sections.title: Before the later southeastern wars
sections.text: The opening keeps a credible upper-Rhone regional identity while treating precise frontiers and leadership as uncertain. Its important routes are already part of the geographical setting. The political outcomes associated with later Mediterranean armies remain future developments, not the reason the inhabitants exist or an unavoidable script for their campaign history.

helvetii.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
helvetii.text: The Helvetian faction uses a northern Alpine and plateau association familiar from later sources, but its exact earlier distribution requires caution. Spring 278 BCE belongs to the wider La Tène-period world, not to Caesar's migration narrative of 58 BCE. The regional communities represented here have their own settlement and exchange histories without necessarily sharing the full later Helvetian political organization.
helvetii.homeland: The northern Alpine zone and plateau associated with later Helvetian geography
helvetii.politicalForm: Regional communities; exact early range and common leadership are uncertain

sections.title: The earlier northern Alpine world
sections.text: Later written descriptions of the Helvetii reflect a particular stage of movement and political development. They should not fix every third-century boundary. Archaeology provides a longer regional history, including the material traditions named after La Tène. The archaeological label is useful for chronology and connections, but does not identify one single people or prove that all related objects belonged to a Helvetian state.

sections.title: Plateau routes and Alpine connections
sections.text: Lakes, river systems and approaches to the Alps connect settlement districts with several wider regions. Local communities participate in movement of goods and people without requiring a unified mountain kingdom. The famous site of La Tène has its own dated deposits and interpretations. Its entire assemblage and final appearance should not be treated as a direct inventory of one faction in 278.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: The record does not identify a complete spring political hierarchy. Community organization, social differentiation and regional cooperation are plausible, but later subdivisions and named leaders cannot simply be moved backward. A military or migration episode described centuries later reveals one historical situation rather than a permanent constitution. The opening therefore leaves room for political development within a substantially inhabited landscape.

sections.title: Between Alpine and Gallic regions
sections.text: Connections reach toward the upper Rhone, other Gallic communities and lands north of the Alps. Cultural similarity does not establish an all-Celtic alliance, and later migration routes are not mandatory opening movements. Roman intervention in Caesar's period is distant future history. The important early setting is the network of neighbouring populations and routes rather than an already established Roman frontier.

sections.title: A qualified early regional association
sections.text: The faction retains a recognizable northern Alpine identity while the exact third-century homeland remains qualified. The opening is not a replay of 58 BCE and does not begin with its named leaders or diplomatic obligations. Archaeological depth and later historical visibility are both preserved without pretending they document the same moment.

dumnonii.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
dumnonii.text: The Dumnonian faction represents communities of southwestern Britain, not a documented kingdom whose later rulers can be carried backward into 278 BCE. The region's Iron Age history includes farming settlements, defended places and connections along the Atlantic and Channel coasts. Its position gives it a distinctive maritime setting even though the named Dumnonii become clearer in sources written centuries after the opening.
dumnonii.homeland: Southwestern Britain, broadly the later Devon–Cornwall association
dumnonii.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age regional communities under a later recorded name

sections.title: An earlier southwestern population
sections.text: Local settlement history continues from the Bronze Age into the Iron Age rather than beginning with Ptolemy's list of peoples. The later Dumnonian name provides orientation, but not a founding date or certain early royal succession. Medieval Dumnonia belongs to another political world. Neither its rulers nor its later boundaries establish the institutions of the third-century communities represented here.

sections.title: Peninsula and coastal routes
sections.text: The southwestern peninsula combines inland farming districts with access to Channel and Atlantic movement. Defended sites differ in size and chronology; not every later Cornish enclosure already exists in the opening. Metal resources contribute to the wider history of exchange, but should not become an assumed state monopoly over all British tin or proof that Greek merchants rule local settlements.

sections.title: Community life in 278 BCE
sections.text: The most secure starting units are households, local settlements and relationships between communities. Roundhouse traditions and agricultural organization reveal a social landscape more substantial than a loose band of warriors. Exact leadership titles and the reach of shared authority are unknown. A local elite can exist without a documented peninsula-wide crown, and the later ethnonym need not correspond to one fixed early state.

sections.title: The Channel and Atlantic neighbourhood
sections.text: Connections toward other British regions, Ireland and the continental coast are possible through established maritime routes. They do not prove permanent alliance or a single Celtic government spanning the sea. Rome is not an occupying power in Britain in 278, and its later provincial geography does not define the region. External relationships are primarily among indigenous communities and those participating in exchange.

sections.title: A regional start before named kingdoms
sections.text: The opening preserves a credible southwestern population and a recognizable later label. Its history is rooted in the inhabited Middle Iron Age landscape rather than an invented migration of foreign rulers. Precise tribal boundaries and named dynasties remain less secure than the region's settlement traditions and maritime position.

durotriges.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
durotriges.text: The Durotrigan setting lies in southern Britain, especially the Dorset-associated landscape of substantial hillforts, farms and routes toward the Channel. Around 278 BCE the region is already inhabited by organized communities, but the later named people, coinages and encounter with Roman conquest belong to a different stage of its history. The opening must distinguish those phases rather than collapse them into one timeless tribal kingdom.
durotriges.homeland: Southern Britain, principally the later Dorset-associated setting
durotriges.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age settlement communities; later Durotrigan unity is not assumed

sections.title: The development of a hillfort landscape
sections.text: Sites such as Maiden Castle demonstrate long and changing occupation, with earlier activity preceding the major Iron Age settlement. Expansion of defences and internal arrangements occurred in stages. This history shows organized local communities before the Roman conquest narrative, but does not prove that every large hillfort was the capital of a separate kingdom or already shared one Durotrigan government.

sections.title: Chalk country and the Channel
sections.text: Farming districts, stored agricultural produce and connections between settlements are fundamental to the regional landscape. The Channel supplies another direction of movement rather than a barrier to all contact. Hillforts can serve several social roles as well as defence. Their most imposing surviving appearance should not automatically be assigned to 278 without regard to the site's individual chronology.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Households and communities organize cultivation, livestock and local authority. Defensive construction suggests collective resources, but does not identify a known starting king. Later coin production and social relationships cannot simply be moved backward. Archaeology gives evidence of organized everyday life while leaving the exact scale of political coordination across the region less securely documented.

sections.title: Southern British connections
sections.text: Neighbouring regions and cross-Channel exchange create opportunities for contact without requiring a single southern confederation. The Roman army's later arrival is not an existing threat from a nearby province in 278. Famous interpretations of conquest violence at Maiden Castle concern much later evidence and debate. They should not define the present condition of every community in the starting region.

sections.title: Before the coinage and conquest period
sections.text: The faction's identity provides a later historical name for an earlier inhabited region. Its starting strength comes from established local societies, not a fictional treasury of later coins or a pre-assigned Roman war. The exact third-century political relationships among hillforts and surrounding communities remain qualified.

catuvellauni.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
catuvellauni.text: The Catuvellaunian faction represents an earlier southeastern British setting associated with the later powerful people of that name. In 278 BCE the well-known royal households and coinages of the late Iron Age are still far in the future. The historical foundation is instead a landscape of farming communities, enclosures and regional contacts whose precise collective identity is not recorded by contemporary written sources.
catuvellauni.homeland: Southeastern British interior, broadly the later Hertfordshire–Chiltern association
catuvellauni.politicalForm: Middle Iron Age communities; the later dynastic state is not projected backward

sections.title: Before the later southeastern dynasties
sections.text: The later political community is known through Roman accounts, archaeology and coinage of a much later period. The age of Cassivellaunus and the subsequent dynasties cannot serve as a complete early history for 278. Earlier local occupation is well established, while the timing and process through which broad political identities formed remain open questions rather than a recorded founding charter.

sections.title: An inland southeastern landscape
sections.text: The Chiltern-facing and neighbouring districts connect agricultural communities with routes toward the Thames and other regions. Hillforts and enclosed sites belong to different phases, and some were abandoned before the opening while other forms of settlement continued. The developed late Iron Age centres associated with Verlamion or Camulodunum should not appear as fully formed starting capitals.

sections.title: Internal conditions in 278 BCE
sections.text: Household organization, access to land and local networks supply a more grounded picture than an invented royal court. Differences in status are compatible with the archaeological evidence, but the exact number and authority of leaders are unknown. It would be misleading to transfer named coin-issuing rulers, their family disputes or later territorial ambitions into this earlier Middle Iron Age community grouping.

sections.title: Regional contacts before Roman intervention
sections.text: The Thames-connected world and neighbouring southeastern communities create channels for exchange and competition. Cross-Channel contact does not establish the later political relationships surrounding Caesar's expeditions. There is no Roman client kingdom here in 278. Nor does a recognizable later faction name prove that the region already commands all territories acquired by its much later rulers.

sections.title: A recognizable label for an earlier society
sections.text: The opening uses the existing regional identity while preserving the chronological distance from its best-known rulers. Local communities remain present without a fabricated dynasty or an already consolidated southeastern kingdom. Later expansion is historical perspective, not a starting entitlement over neighbouring peoples.

iceni.scopeNote: The name and regional association are recorded in later sources. This opening represents earlier local communities, without assuming the later political structure.
